chapter: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
title: Color consciousness and teasing about Blackness
summary: Dance and Ramirez discuss prejudice against Rex for being big and dark, and the era's jokes about color versus later talk of Black pride.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: He rather demanded to be treated with respect. But of course, you know, he was fat and he was Black, and that was like a double-strike against him, because he didn't look like an intelligent man somehow. Do you know what I mean?
Well, to me it appeared just the other way around. I thought he was the classiest thing... You know, when Black Is Beautiful hit... He was...
Do you know how they used to say "blacker than me" and everything like that, all that old nonsense...
I'm sure that Rex, being intelligent, suffered to some extent from that.

Well, in those days they had a way that they would make sort of a humorous remark about color, you know. If you'd say, "Well, I just saw so-and-so," then "Well, you got a black way of showing it." And if you said, "Clark Gable," instead you would "Dark Gable," you know. And that went on... I guess you sort of had to be in the In Crowd to do that kind of thing, you know. It wasn't the way I...

They made fun about Blacks. But on the other hand, too, in actions they exalted something different. You know what I mean? In action. Now it seems to be the other way around. [LAUGHS] They talk a lot of talk about Black is this, but when they...actually they Tom more than the older...
